name: TPS74801DRCR
title: 1.5 A low-dropout linear regulator with bias input and programmable soft-start
summary: The TPS74801 (family name TPS748) is an adjustable 1.5 A linear regulator with an NMOS pass device. A separate BIAS supply of 2.7 V to 5.5 V runs the reference, error amplifier and gate drive, so the power input can sit as low as 0.8 V and the dropout from IN is 50 to 60 mV typical at full load when BIAS is at least 3.25 V above the output. The output is set from 0.8 V to 3.6 V with two resistors, is stable with 2.2 µF or more of any capacitor type, and ramps up monotonically at a rate set by one capacitor on SS. It has an enable input with hysteresis and deglitch, an open-drain power-good output, current limit, thermal shutdown and an output pulldown when disabled. Two die are shipped under the same numbers, a legacy chip and a new chip; parts ending in M3 carry only the new chip.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit (adjustable)
circuits.description: The basic adjustable regulator. IN and EN share the input rail with a 1 µF capacitor; BIAS has its own rail and 1 µF. R1 from OUT to FB and R2 from FB to ground set VOUT = 0.8 × (1 + R1 / R2), with values from the resistor table. A 1 nF capacitor on SS sets the soft-start ramp, R3 pulls the open-drain PG output up to VOUT, and 10 µF on OUT keeps the loop stable.

parts.note: upper divider resistor; see the resistor table
lower divider resistor, 4.99 kΩ or less

notes: With VBIAS and EN present and no VIN, about 50 µA flows out of OUT; if OUT sees more than 10 kΩ to ground, including the divider, this current can charge the output.

circuits.title: Soft-start delay with an RC circuit on EN
circuits.description: R from BIAS to EN and C from EN to ground hold the enable off until VBIAS has risen, so the soft-start ramp begins only after the bias rail is up. The same RC can drive EN from VIN instead.

circuits.title: FPGA I/O supply at 1.5 V with a bias rail
circuits.description: Steps a 1.8 V input down to 1.5 V at up to 1.5 A for FPGA I/O, with BIAS taken from a 5 V ± 5 % rail. With BIAS at least 3.25 V above the output the IN dropout is at most 165 mV, which allows the 1.8 V to 1.5 V step; efficiency is about 83 %. R1 = 4.12 kΩ and R2 = 4.75 kΩ give 1.5 V, the capacitors are the minimum sizes, and 1 nF on SS gives a start-up of about 1.8 ms.

circuits.title: FPGA I/O supply at 1.5 V without a bias rail
circuits.description: With only a 3.3 V rail available, IN and BIAS are tied together on it and the output is 1.5 V at up to 1.5 A. BIAS then sets the dropout, so this is inefficient (about 45 %); the load draws current only in short bursts at 5 % duty, so heating is not a concern. R1 = 4.12 kΩ and R2 = 4.75 kΩ set 1.5 V, CIN and CBIAS are 4.7 µF each, COUT is 2.2 µF and CSS is 1 nF for about 1.8 ms start-up.

operation.text: An NMOS pass transistor is driven from the BIAS supply, which also powers the reference and control circuits. This lets the regulator work from very low input and output voltages, makes stability largely independent of the output capacitor (any type of 2.2 µF or more), and gives a fast transient response at low VIN.

The same orderable numbers ship with either a legacy chip (CSO: DLN) or a new chip (CSO: RFB); parts with the M3 suffix carry only the new chip. The reel label's CSO code identifies the die. The new chip has tighter accuracy (±1 % against ±2 %), lower dropout (100 mV max against 165 mV), lower shutdown and PG leakage currents, a 530 nA soft-start current against 440 nA, and an internal 833 Ω pulldown in both.

EN is active high: below 0.4 V the regulator is off, above 1.1 V it is on. The threshold is typically 0.8 V and falls about 1 mV/°C, with process spread making up the rest of the window. Hysteresis (typically 50 mV) and a deglitch filter let EN follow a slowly rising analog signal, such as another regulator's output, without chatter. For exact turn-on timing drive EN with a fast edge. Unused, EN can be tied to IN or BIAS; if tied to IN, connect it near the largest input capacitor so droops on IN do not trip it.
When disabled, the output is pulled to GND through an internal 833 Ω resistor, discharging COUT with the time constant given in the equations.

PG is open drain and can be pulled up to any rail of 5.5 V or less. It needs at least 1.1 V on BIAS to be valid. PG releases when VOUT exceeds VIT + VHYS and pulls low when VOUT falls below VIT, when VBIAS drops under 1.9 V, or when the device is disabled. Keep the sink current at 1 mA or less, which means a pull-up of 10 kΩ to 1 MΩ. PG may float if unused.

The current limit is trimmed and stays flat over temperature and supply. Surges of up to 2 A are delivered in regulation; in a short circuit the limit acts in about 10 µs. It protects against overload and is not meant for continuous use above the 1.5 A rating, which degrades reliability.

The output turns off when the junction reaches about 160 °C and back on at about 140 °C, so under sustained overload it cycles. Keep the junction at 125 °C or below; for margin, thermal shutdown should only trip at least 40 °C above the highest expected ambient with worst-case load. Running into thermal shutdown repeatedly degrades reliability.

Normal regulation needs IN and BIAS above their minimums, EN having passed its rising threshold without falling below the falling one, load below current limit and junction below its maximum. If IN drops below VOUT plus dropout the part is in dropout: the output follows the input less the dropout and transient response is much worse because the pass device is in triode. Low IN or BIAS, low EN or overtemperature disables it.

The error amplifier follows the voltage on the SS capacitor, charged by ISS, until it passes the 0.8 V reference, giving a linear, monotonic ramp that limits inrush into large output capacitance. With a big COUT the current limit may set the ramp instead. The largest recommended CSS is 15 nF: larger values do no harm but may not fully discharge when EN is pulsed quickly. CSS must be low leakage (X7R, X5R or C0G). A feed-forward capacitor is another way to slow start-up.

IN, BIAS and EN may come up in any order without damage. For the programmed soft-start to act, EN tied to IN works when VIN is above 1.1 V and both supplies rise faster than the soft-start ramp. If the supplies rise more slowly, the output follows the slower one less dropout. With EN tied to BIAS, soft-start works as set provided IN is up before BIAS. If BIAS and EN are up before IN and soft-start has finished, VOUT follows VIN; if not finished, VOUT follows VIN until it meets the soft-start voltage. An RC on EN or an external enable signal can delay turn-on until both supplies are present.

Any output capacitor type of 2.2 µF or more is stable, including several in parallel. Input capacitance depends on source impedance: at least 1 µF on IN and 0.1 µF on BIAS, or 4.7 µF when IN and BIAS share a supply. Use low-ESR ceramic X5R or X7R parts placed close to the pins.

Where VIN − VOUT is under 300 mV the input supply can limit transient response, and extra input capacitance helps more than extra output capacitance. With a stiff input, more output capacitance reduces overshoot and undershoot. Since 2.2 µF is enough for stability, the load's own local bypass capacitors may be all that is needed.

VIN dropout applies with a separate bias rail at least 3.25 V above VOUT (for example 5 V − 5 % with a 1.5 V output); more bias headroom lowers it further. VBIAS dropout applies when IN and BIAS are tied: BIAS supplies the pass-transistor gate drive, so it must be 1.6 V above VOUT, which makes the tied connection inefficient; watch the package power limit.

After soft-start the SS capacitor filters the reference, which produces most of the noise. A 1 nF CSS halves the noise, to about 30 µVRMS at 1.2 V out (10 Hz to 100 kHz); more capacitance gains little. Noise scales with the output voltage.

IN may go up to 5.5 V as long as BIAS is at least 1.62 V above it and dropout is met. Feed IN from a low-impedance source with at least 1 µF near the pin, and BIAS from a similar source with its own 1 µF or more; 4.7 µF if they are tied. A pi filter or ferrite bead ahead of the input capacitor raises PSRR at high frequency.

Place the IN and BIAS capacitors as near the device as possible to cut droop and parasitic inductance. Connect the top of R1 close to the load for best accuracy and transient response, and keep COUT near the regulator. If BIAS is tied to IN, take BIAS from near the input supply's sense point. In the RGW example the input and output ground planes stay on the same side of the board for heat spreading, with thermal vias under the pad.

Heat leaves mainly through the exposed pad into the PCB on both packages. The pad may be grounded or left floating but must be soldered to enough copper. Find the needed RθJA from the maximum ambient and dissipation and use the RθJA-versus-copper-area curve as a guide to board area; its value at 9 in² (a 3 in × 3 in board) is the JEDEC standard figure. On a real board ΨJT and ΨJB, which barely change with board size, give TJ from a measured top or board temperature (an infrared thermometer is suitable).
